tier_reason: The cited Quarkslab post only supports C. Its clang++-5.0 -O3 line belongs to an assembly listing, not the benchmark, and the repo's Feb-2018 benchmarks/Makefile builds with $(CXX) -O2. A is kept on stronger third-party evidence: arXiv 2602.22506 (Myhal & Serang, 2026) benchmarks frozen::unordered_map against std::unordered_map with public MIT code (figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.31416038: main_frozen.cpp, main.cpp, codon_to_amino_acid.cpp, stock_to_price.cpp, Makefile), g++ 15.2.1 -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native, on an Intel Core i5-1240P.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Construction+lookup runtime, frozen::unordered_map vs std::unordered_map: element-symbol->mass demo 44.9 us vs 89.6 us (~2.0x), codon->amino-acid demo 1365.5 us vs 1746.8 us (~1.28x), ticker->price update demo 15804.5 us vs 21228.1 us (~1.34x) (ratios derived from page data, Figure 2 averages)
corrections.baseline: std::unordered_map (arXiv 2602.22506 demos); std::set and std::unordered_set in the author's first-party 2018 Quarkslab microbenchmark
corrections.workload: Three application demos from arXiv 2602.22506: 1,024 random lookups in an 84-key element-symbol->atomic-mass map (each lookup timed individually); translation of 65,536 random codons through a 64-key codon->amino-acid map; 64 x 4,042 random price updates in a 4,042-key ticker->price map. Reported time = runtime construction + lookup, averaged over repeated runs.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-1240P laptop (runs under nice -n -20, chrt -f 98, ASLR disabled)
corrections.caveats: arXiv 2602.22506 is a non-peer-reviewed preprint about a competing library (static_maps), which beats frozen in all three demos. The frozen-vs-std ratios are derived from its Figure 2 averages; the Figure 2 caption is misprinted as map vs std::map. The std::unordered_map timings include runtime construction, which frozen does at compile time. The element demo wraps every single lookup in high_resolution_clock calls, so its ~2.0x partly reflects construction and timer overhead; the lookup-dominated codon demo shows ~1.28x. Keys differ: std::unordered_map<std::string_view,...> with std::hash vs frozen::basic_string with frozen's own hash. The version of the frozen copy bundled in the artifact is not stated. libstdc++ is inferred from the g++ build with no -stdlib flag. The earlier first-party Quarkslab post (Serge Guelton, 20 Feb 2018) reports frozen::set/unordered_set vs std::set/unordered_set on 32 keys, where each reported time is one pass of 32 lookups: int unordered_set 173 vs 544 ns (~3.1x), absent keys 131 vs 500 ns (~3.8x); int set 58 vs 153 ns (~2.6x); strings x1.7 (set) to x3.3 (unordered_set, absent key). That post states the CPU (i7-6600U) but not the benchmark compiler or flags, and its std string containers hold frozen::string keys hashed by frozen's own std::hash specialization.

notes: The Quarkslab numbers are verbatim on the page, but the record misattributed the clang++-5.0 -O3 line: it belongs to the assembly listing, not the benchmark. I replaced benchmark_url with the independent arXiv 2602.22506 preprint and its public figshare artifact, which keeps tier A and compares directly against std::unordered_map. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 1,578 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: The only number is a first-party prose claim in the mph_map.h header ('about 10%-50% faster than unordered_map' for >100k URLs). No results, compiler, flags or hardware are published. A harness exists (cxxmph/bm_map.cc runs mph_map against std::unordered_map), but its URLS100k dataset is not in the repo and no output is given, so the claim stays at C.

corrections.baseline: std::unordered_map (cxxmph's dense_hash_map / sparse_hash_map are its own flavors named after the sparsehash classes; cxxmph/bm_map.cc benchmarks only against std::unordered_map)
corrections.workload: Header claim: lookups over large (>100k) URL key sets. The repo harness cxxmph/bm_map.cc builds and searches ~100k URL keys (URLS100k file, not shipped) with 10M searches at 0% and 90% miss ratio, plus 100k uint64 keys with 10M searches. It compares cxxmph::mph_map (BDZ minimal perfect hash behind an unordered_map-compatible interface) with std::unordered_map<StringPiece, StringPiece, Murmur3StringPiece>.
corrections.caveats: The 10-50% figure is a prose claim in the mph_map.h header. No results, compiler, flags or hardware are published; the header only advises -O3 -DNDEBUG. The same header warns: 'Those classes are not necessarily faster than their existing counterparts. Benchmark your code before using it.' A benchmark harness exists (cxxmph/bm_map.cc, bm_common.cc, benchmark.cc), but the URLS100k dataset is not in the repo. zvelo/cmph is a 2012 import: its last code change is 2012-12-05, and the 2017 commit only deleted a config file. The author's own repo, github.com/bonitao/cmph (Davi de Castro Reis), has the same header and was last updated 2026-04-27. License: COPYING says dual 'LGPL version 2' / MPL 1.1, but the LGPL-2 file contains LGPL 2.1 text. GitHub reports NOASSERTION, and the files do not say whether the LGPL is '-only' or '-or-later'. In cxxmph, stringpiece.h is BSD and MurmurHash is MIT.

notes: The quote is verbatim on the page. Consider changing repo_url to the author's active upstream, https://github.com/bonitao/cmph (20 stars, last commit 2026-04-27). zvelo/cmph (91 stars) is a stale 2012 import, not a GitHub fork, so maintenance_status 'abandoned' is correct for this URL. Metadata checked: 91 stars, last commit 2017-03-02, not archived; license kept as recorded because the LGPL variant cannot be pinned down exactly.

tier_reason: The README numbers are first-party and come from public bench code (bench/bench.cc, bench/compare.cc, bench/dispatch_field_types.cc; CMakeLists.txt compiles them with -O3). GCC 11 is stated, but the hardware is given only as 'x86_64' with no CPU model, so the tier is C, not A.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (README plus bench/), not independently reproduced. Hardware is stated only as x86_64, with no CPU model. In bench/compare.cc, the 'if-ladder' is a runtime loop over the key array, and the 'switch (binary search)' column is std::lower_bound over a sorted vector, not compiler-generated switch code. std::unordered_map<uint32_t,uint32_t> uses the default std::hash. The string-dispatch benchmark uses a 50/50 mix of members and non-members (200k lookups, best of 15) against std::unordered_map<std::string,int> and std::set<std::string>. The README does not say which hash (fnv1a or wordwise) produced its 21 ns 'hash + verify' row. The stop-word benchmark has no published numbers, only a claim that it 'edges ahead of gperf'. libstdc++ is inferred from GCC 11, which has no -stdlib option in this build. gperf, frozen and trie numbers come from the same first-party harness.

notes: All claimed numbers are verbatim in the README Benchmarks section. Derived ratios vs std::unordered_map: ~2.5-2.7x for integer keys; ~1.4x (hash+verify) or ~1.6x (hash-only) for strings; ~3.9x vs std::set. Metadata checked: MIT, 37 stars, last commit 2026-07-12 (the README rewrite that added these tables), not archived, not a fork.
